title: The Passive Income Scam
summary: Argues passive income is really investment income (needs capital) or entrepreneurial income (needs effort); easy strategies get arbitraged away, and the sellers profit from the pitch.

assertions.quote: passive income really just means front loading your work not eliminating it
you would need to accumulate 600 000 in net savings not an easy first step for passive income
it also comes with large unexpected costs and risks like a broken water heater a hole in the roof
as for trading Bots they don't work

verdicts.note: The FTC alleged few consumers ever made money from DK Automation's schemes, which included its crypto trading bot; an enforcement allegation, not a performance measurement.

assertions.quote: the average small business owner Works twice as hard as their employees with 25 percent working at least 60 hours a week

verdicts.note: Surveys consistently report small business owners working longer hours than employees.

Incorporated self-employed work about 340 more hours a year than comparable full-time, full-year salaried workers and the unincorporated about 285 more after controls (raw CPS: 2,347 annual hours for incorporated vs 1,981 for salaried); the comparison is with salaried workers generally rather than owners' own employees.

assertions.quote: you can bet that there will be thousands of others doing the exact same thing possibly with the exact same product
you can bet that the opportunity has probably already passed
nearly 90 of that will never pass the 1000 view Mark at which point you might make a few dollars

verdicts.note: View distributions on YouTube are heavily skewed with most uploads getting few views.

A random sample of 10,016 YouTube videos found 86.93% had fewer than a thousand views and 65.44% fewer than a hundred, confirming the first half; the paper does not measure creator income or test whether luck explains it.

assertions.quote: nearly 90 of e-commerce stores fail within the first four months

verdicts.note: Taylor quotes SBA figures that 44% of small businesses survive at least four years and 31% at least seven, and an NFIB survey finding 64.2% failed within ten years; general small-business data, not specific to online stores.

Of US private establishments opened in the year to March 2015, 79.6% survived one year, 61.4% three years, 50.2% five years and 34.7% ten years (other cohorts are similar), so about half close within five years and two-thirds within ten; 'most fail within a few years' overstates it, establishment exits include sales and relocations rather than only failures, and there is no online-store breakdown.

BLS defines an establishment as a single economic unit such as a store or factory, typically at one physical location, in contrast to a firm or company, which may consist of one or more establishments; establishment survival counts places of business, not businesses.

BLS age and survival data are measured at the establishment level, not the firm level: a chain store's new branch is a new opening for the establishment tables though only an expansion for the firm, so the survival tables are not a business failure rate.

A BLS closing is an establishment that had positive employment and then reports none (or zero) in the current quarter; the definition records that payroll employment stopped at that unit, not why, so an exit is not necessarily a failure.

BLS links establishment records across quarters by state UI id, and where the id changes through predecessor and successor records (including a change in ownership or a restructuring) or a match on name, address and phone, so a sold or reorganised establishment is meant to continue rather than count as a closing; unmatched records would still appear as an exit.
